claims.claim: The C-terminal domain of Treacle harbors additional NLSs, a UBF binding site, and a lysine-rich LCR (K-rich LCR) at the terminus, which also functions as a nucleolar localization signal (NoLS).
claims.source: The CD harbors additional NLSs, a UBF binding site, and a lysine-rich LCR (K-rich LCR) at the terminus, which also functions as a nucleolar localization signal (NoLS) (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Stated as a structural characteristic of Treacle and shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: A recombinant fragment of Treacle (amino acids 291–426) forms liquid-like condensates in vitro in the presence of 5% polyethylene glycol.
claims.source: In vitro experiments demonstrated that this recombinant fragment formed liquid-like condensates in the presence of 5% polyethylene glycol (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro condensation assay shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: In vitro Treacle condensates exhibit a spherical morphology.
claims.source: These condensates exhibited a spherical morphology and frequently underwent fusion events (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: In vitro Treacle condensates frequently undergo fusion events.
claims.source: These condensates exhibited a spherical morphology and frequently underwent fusion events (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Opto-Treacle forms foci in nucleoli in the absence of blue light.
claims.source: Expression of this opto-Treacle chimeric protein in HeLa cells revealed foci formation in nucleoli in the absence of blue light, consistent with Treacle's natural tendency to occupy FCs (Figure 2D; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1B for the controls).
claims.evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Under blue light, opto-Treacle forms multiple small foci throughout the nucleoplasm.
claims.source: Under blue light, opto-Treacle formed multiple small foci throughout the nucleoplasm (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: At low expression levels (16–24 hr post-transfection), Treacle's fusion protein forms foci only in nucleoli.
claims.source: At low expression levels (16–24 hr post-transfection), Treacle's fusion protein formed foci only in nucleoli, reflecting its natural occupation of FCs (Figure 2E, top panel; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: At increased expression levels (48–72 hr post-transfection), Treacle's fusion protein forms large spherical structures in the nucleoplasm.
claims.source: However, at increased expression levels (48–72 hr post-transfection), it began to form large spherical structures in the nucleoplasm (Figure 2E, bottom panel; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The formation of large nuclear condensates at high Treacle expression levels is not due to oligomerization of the fluorescent protein tags.
claims.source: The formation of these structures could not be attributed to the oligomerization of 2S or GFP, as comparable large nuclear condensates were observed at high levels of Treacle expression, even in the absence of a fused fluorescent protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Both intranucleolar and extranucleolar Treacle-2S foci exhibit a spherical shape with an aspect ratio close to one.
claims.source: Both intranucleolar and extranucleolar Treacle-2S foci, induced by low and high levels of fusion protein expression respectively, exhibited a spherical shape with an aspect ratio close to one, suggesting susceptibility to surface tension (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by 3D shape analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Transmission electron microscopy confirms the internal homogeneity of Treacle condensates.
claims.source: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed the internal homogeneity of Treacle condensates, showing circular structures with homogeneous protein content without any electron-dense or -light regions inside the condensates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by TEM images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Nucleolar caps form during AMD-induced rDNA transcriptional repression due to the fusion of intranucleolar Treacle-2S foci.
claims.source: Our observations revealed that nucleolar caps form during AMD-induced (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G; Figure 2—video 1) or DNA damage-induced (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H; Figure 2—video 7) rDNA transcriptional repression due to the fusion of intranucleolar Treacle-2S foci.
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: Extranucleolar biomolecular condensates from highly overexpressed Treacle-2S frequently fuse.
claims.source: Prolonged live-cell imaging further demonstrated that extranucleolar biomolecular condensates from highly overexpressed Treacle-2S frequently fuse, indicating dynamic clustering (Figure 2G; Figure 2—video 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Half-FRAP analysis of Treacle-2S-formed FCs reveals an increase in signal intensity in the bleached half accompanied by a proportional decrease in fluorescence in the non-bleached half.
claims.source: Half-FRAP analysis revealed an increase in signal intensity in the bleached half of Treacle-2S-formed FCs, accompanied by a proportional decrease in fluorescence in the non-bleached half (Figure 2H and I; Figure 2—video 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by half-FRAP data shown in Figure 2H and I.

claims.claim: Full-FRAP analysis of Treacle dynamics within FCs reveals a slow recovery rate.
claims.source: Full-FRAP analysis of Treacle dynamics within FCs revealed a slow recovery rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), suggesting preferential internal mixing.
claims.evidence: Supported by full-FRAP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Molecular exchange in Treacle FCs occurs between the two halves of the condensate without significant exchange across the boundary separating the condensate from the surrounding phase.
claims.source: This indicates that molecular exchange occurs between the two halves of the condensate without significant exchange across the boundary separating the condensate from the surrounding phase.
claims.evidence: Inferred from FRAP analysis showing internal mixing without external exchange.

claims.claim: Fluorescence in the non-bleached region of Treacle FCs decreases to approximately half its initial value during half-FRAP, suggesting near-complete internal mixing within the coacervate.
claims.source: Notably, fluorescence in the non-bleached region decreased to approximately half its initial value, suggesting near-complete internal mixing within the coacervate.
claims.evidence: Inferred from half-FRAP data showing equilibration of fluorescence between halves.

claims.claim: Comparable full- and half-FRAP dynamics were observed for AMD-induced nucleolar caps.
claims.source: Comparable full- and half-FRAP dynamics were observed for AMD-induced nucleolar caps Figure 2J and K; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; Figure 2—video 4 and extranucleolar condensates formed under elevated Treacle-2S expression (Figure 2L and M; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; Figure 2—video 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2J, K, L, M, and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The largest extranucleolar condensates exhibit reduced Treacle molecular dynamics, suggesting more gel-like properties.
claims.source: Furthermore, the largest extranucleolar condensates exhibited reduced Treacle molecular dynamics, suggesting more gel-like properties (Figure 2L and M; Figure 2—figure supplement 2D; Figure 2—video 6).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2L, M, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Treacle condensates undergo a liquid-to-gel phase transition over time or upon reaching a critical protein concentration within the condensate.
claims.source: Presumably, Treacle condensates undergo a liquid-to-gel phase transition over time or upon reaching a critical protein concentration within the condensate.
claims.evidence: Speculated based on observed changes in molecular dynamics in larger condensates.

claims.claim: The Δ1–83 mutant demonstrates condensation properties indistinguishable from full-length Treacle.
claims.source: The Δ1–83 mutant demonstrated condensation properties indistinguishable from full-length Treacle: it concentrated in FCs, formed stable nucleolar caps during transcriptional repression, and, upon increased expression levels, generated numerous large extranucleolar condensates (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, D, and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The Δ1–83 mutant exhibits a high rate of molecular exchange in all types of model condensates, similar to full-length Treacle.
claims.source: Using partial FRAP analysis, we further demonstrated that, similar to full-length Treacle (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C), the Δ1–83 mutant exhibited a high rate of molecular exchange in all types of model condensates (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by partial FRAP data shown in Figure 3B, C, and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The Δ83–1121 mutant exhibits significantly compromised condensation properties.
claims.source: As expected, the Δ83–1121 mutant exhibited significantly compromised condensation properties.
claims.evidence: Stated as an observation from experimental data.

claims.claim: Under low expression levels, the Δ83–1121 mutant fails to concentrate in FCs.
claims.source: Under low expression levels, it failed to concentrate in FCs (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) and diffusely localized in the nucleolus while still maintaining a high molecular dynamics rate (Figure 3E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy and FRAP data shown in Figure 3D, E, F, and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: During rDNA transcriptional repression, the Δ83–1121 mutant does not form classical nucleolar caps but partially redistributes between the nucleolar periphery and nucleoplasm.
claims.source: During rDNA transcriptional repression, the Δ83–1121 mutant did not form classical nucleolar caps but partially redistributed between the nucleolar periphery and nucleoplasm, where it began to form condensates (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Nucleoplasmic condensates of the Δ83–1121 mutant, formed due to nucleolar transcriptional repression, begin to transition into a solid-like state.
claims.source: Partial FRAP analysis revealed that nucleoplasmic condensates of the Δ83–1121 mutant, formed due to nucleolar transcriptional repression, began to transition into a solid-like state (Figure 3E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by partial FRAP data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claims.claim: Under high expression levels, the Δ83–1121 mutant no longer forms distinct extranucleolar condensates but merges into a unified pan-nuclear solid network.
claims.source: A similar liquid-solid transition was observed for the Δ83–1121 mutant under high expression levels. In this case, it no longer formed distinct extranucleolar condensates but merged into a unified pan-nuclear solid network (Figure 3D–F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy and FRAP data shown in Figure 3D, E, F, and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The RD deletion alters Treacle's interaction patterns, making its phase separation properties more reliant on rRNA and other nucleolar proteins.
claims.source: This behavior suggests that the RD deletion alters Treacle's interaction patterns, making its phase separation properties more reliant on rRNA and other nucleolar proteins.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the altered condensation behavior of the Δ83–1121 mutant.

claims.claim: The Δ1121–1488 mutant fails to condense.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, the Δ1121–1488 mutant also failed to condense.
claims.evidence: Stated as an observation from experimental data.

claims.claim: When equipped with an artificial NLS from the SV40 virus, the Δ1121–1488 mutant successfully translocates into the nucleus but remains diffusely distributed throughout the nucleoplasm.
claims.source: When equipped with an artificial NLS from the SV40 virus, it successfully translocated into the nucleus; however, it remained diffusely distributed throughout the nucleoplasm, even under high expression conditions (Figure 3G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Without the CD, Treacle cannot undergo autonomous condensation, likely relying on the CD as a nucleation factor.
claims.source: Therefore, without the CD, Treacle cannot undergo autonomous condensation, likely relying on the CD as a nucleation factor.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the failure of the Δ1121–1488 mutant to condense.

claims.claim: The intracellular Treacle condensation depends on a cooperative interaction between RD and CD.
claims.source: Collectively, these results suggest that the intracellular Treacle condensation depends on a cooperative interaction between RD and CD.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the condensation defects observed in mutants lacking either RD or CD.

claims.claim: Treatment with ammonium acetate disrupts both FCs and extranucleolar condensates formed at low and high Treacle expression levels, respectively.
claims.source: Treatment with the cell-permeable salt ammonium acetate disrupted both FCs and extranucleolar condensates formed at low and high Treacle expression levels, respectively (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Treatment with 1,6-HD does not affect the integrity of Treacle condensates.
claims.source: In contrast, treatment with 1,6-HD did not affect the integrity of Treacle condensates (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The efficiency of Treacle's fragment condensation in vitro remains unchanged in the presence of 1,6-HD.
claims.source: The efficiency of Treacle's fragment condensation in vitro remained unchanged in the presence of 1,6-HD, whereas increasing salt concentration prevented condensation (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro condensation assay shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Increasing salt concentration prevents condensation of Treacle's fragment in vitro.
claims.source: The efficiency of Treacle's fragment condensation in vitro remained unchanged in the presence of 1,6-HD, whereas increasing salt concentration prevented condensation (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro condensation assay shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Condensation of the Treacle RD fragment in vitro is sensitive to changes in pH.
claims.source: Additionally, condensation of the Treacle RD fragment in vitro was sensitive to changes in pH. The optimal efficiency of condensation was observed at pH 7.0, whereas acidification of the medium decreased condensation, and alkalization resulted in the generation of insoluble aggregates (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro condensation assay shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Treacle condensation, both in vitro and in vivo, is primarily governed by electrostatic interactions rather than hydrophobic forces.
claims.source: Therefore, it is clear that Treacle condensation, both in vitro and in vivo, is primarily governed by electrostatic interactions rather than hydrophobic forces.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the sensitivity to salt but not 1,6-HD treatment.

claims.claim: The deletion of the S/E-rich LCRs significantly compromises Treacle's condensation properties.
claims.source: The deletion of the S/E-rich LCRs significantly compromised Treacle's condensation properties.
claims.evidence: Stated as an observation from experimental data.

claims.claim: Like the Δ83–1121 mutant, Treacle ΔSE could not form FCs or nucleolar caps.
claims.source: Like the Δ83–1121 mutant, Treacle ΔSE could not form FCs or nucleolar caps (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), remained in a liquid state within the nucleolus (Figure 4D and E), and underwent a liquid-solid phase transition during nucleolar transcriptional repression or high overexpression levels (Figure 4D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy and FRAP data shown in Figure 4C, D, E, and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The RD determines Treacle's condensation properties through the S/E-rich LCRs.
claims.source: These findings indicate that the RD determines Treacle's condensation properties through the S/E-rich LCRs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the condensation defects observed in the ΔSE mutant.

claims.claim: The ΔNoLS mutant does not localize to the nucleolus but can form individual perinucleolar condensates.
claims.source: In turn, ΔNoLS mutant did not localize to the nucleolus but could form individual perinucleolar condensates (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The volume of ΔNoLS condensates increases significantly with the expression level of ΔNoLS, but their number does not.
claims.source: Interestingly, the volume of these condensates increased significantly with the expression level of ΔNoLS, but their number did not (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The positively charged lysines in the K-rich LCR of the CD act as nucleation points for autonomous Treacle condensate formation.
claims.source: This implies that the positively charged lysines in the K-rich LCR of the CD act as nucleation points for autonomous Treacle condensate formation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the limited number of nucleation sites in ΔNoLS condensates.

claims.claim: All types of ΔNoLS condensates display high molecular dynamics.
claims.source: It is also noteworthy that all types of ΔNoLS condensates displayed high molecular dynamics (Figure 4G and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claims.claim: Molecular exchange within ΔNoLS condensates occurs across the boundary separating the coacervate from the surrounding phase, rather than through internal mixing.
claims.source: In contrast to full-length Treacle condensates, molecular exchange within ΔNoLS condensates occurred across the boundary separating the coacervate from the surrounding phase, rather than through internal mixing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: The K-rich LCR acts as both a nucleation element in Treacle condensate formation and a regulator of Treacle's volumetric dynamics within these condensates.
claims.source: This finding reinforces the role of the K-rich LCR as both a nucleation element in Treacle condensate formation and a regulator of Treacle's volumetric dynamics within these condensates.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the altered dynamics and nucleation behavior of ΔNoLS condensates.

claims.claim: Each S/E-rich LCR, in conjunction with its adjacent linker, within the RD constitutes a strong diblock ampholyte.
claims.source: Indeed, an analysis of the charge distribution along the Treacle amino acid sequence demonstrated that each S/E-rich LCR, in conjunction with its adjacent linker, within the RD constitutes a strong diblock ampholyte, where a positively charged block (linker) is followed by a negatively charged block (S/E-rich LCR; Figure 4I, left panel).
claims.evidence: Supported by charge distribution analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: Scrambling the charges in the RD fully reproduces the condensation-defective phenotype observed in the Δ83–1121 and ΔSE mutants.
claims.source: As expected, scrambling the charges in the RD fully reproduced the condensation-defective phenotype observed in the Δ83–1121 and ΔSE mutants. Treacle CS failed to form FCs or nucleolar caps, instead assembling into a single pan-nuclear network at high overexpression levels (Figure 4J; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Treacle's condensation properties depend not only on the net negative charge within the RD but are critically influenced by the specific distribution of charges within this region.
claims.source: These findings suggest that Treacle's condensation properties depend not only on the net negative charge within the RD but are critically influenced by the specific distribution of charges within this region.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the condensation defects observed in the charge-scrambled mutant.

claims.claim: The cooperative interaction between the RD and CD governs the phase separation properties of Treacle.
claims.source: In summary, our findings demonstrate that the cooperative interaction between the RD and CD governs the phase separation properties of Treacle, whereas the ND plays a negligible role in this process.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the condensation behavior of various deletion mutants.

claims.claim: The ND plays a negligible role in Treacle's phase separation.
claims.source: In summary, our findings demonstrate that the cooperative interaction between the RD and CD governs the phase separation properties of Treacle, whereas the ND plays a negligible role in this process.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the normal condensation behavior of the Δ1–83 mutant.

claims.claim: The positively charged K-rich LCR within the CD facilitates its role as a nucleation site for Treacle condensate formation.
claims.source: The positively charged K-rich LCR within the CD facilitates its role as a nucleation site for Treacle condensate formation, while the alternating charge blocks in the RD stabilize Treacle condensates, ensuring that Treacle behavior remains independent of subnuclear localization or nucleolar transcriptional activity.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the condensation behavior of ΔNoLS and charge-scrambled mutants.

claims.claim: The alternating charge blocks in the RD stabilize Treacle condensates.
claims.source: The positively charged K-rich LCR within the CD facilitates its role as a nucleation site for Treacle condensate formation, while the alternating charge blocks in the RD stabilize Treacle condensates, ensuring that Treacle behavior remains independent of subnuclear localization or nucleolar transcriptional activity.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the condensation behavior of ΔSE and charge-scrambled mutants.

claims.claim: The expressed full-length Treacle exhibits normal nucleolar localization, similar to endogenous Treacle.
claims.source: The expressed full-length Treacle exhibited normal nucleolar localization, similar to endogenous Treacle. It co-localized within the FC with RPA194 and UBF, while FBL was localized in the DFC at the periphery of the FC, and NCL and B23 surrounded the DFC (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Expression of the Δ83–1121 or CS Treacle mutants leads to the dispersal and mixing of FC and DFC components within the nucleolus.
claims.source: In contrast, expression of the Δ83–1121 or CS Treacle mutants led to the dispersal and mixing of FC and DFC components within the nucleolus (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The Δ83–1121 or CS mutants still co-localize with UBF1, but to a significantly lesser extent with RPA194.
claims.source: Despite this, the Δ83–1121 or CS mutants still co-localized with UBF1, but to a significantly lesser extent with RPA194, suggesting a potential loss of their binding interaction.
claims.evidence: Inferred from co-localization analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The Δ83–1121 or CS mutants show partial overlap with NCL, but not with B23.
claims.source: Interestingly, these mutants showed partial overlap with NCL, but not with B23 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by co-localization analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Disrupting Treacle's condensation properties may alter its interaction preferences.
claims.source: These observations suggest that disrupting Treacle's condensation properties may alter its interaction preferences.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the altered co-localization patterns of condensation-defective mutants.

claims.claim: After AMD treatment, full-length Treacle co-localizes with UBF1 and RPA194 at the nucleolar caps.
claims.source: After AMD treatment, full-length Treacle co-localized with UBF1 and RPA194 at the nucleolar caps (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: After AMD treatment, FBL partially merges with the caps formed by full-length Treacle.
claims.source: FBL partially merged with the caps, while NCL and B23 were completely displaced to the nucleolar rim and nucleoplasm (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: After AMD treatment, NCL and B23 are completely displaced to the nucleolar rim and nucleoplasm in cells expressing full-length Treacle.
claims.source: FBL partially merged with the caps, while NCL and B23 were completely displaced to the nucleolar rim and nucleoplasm (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The AMD-induced perinucleolar or nucleoplasmic solid condensates formed by the Δ83–1121 or CS Treacle mutants still co-localize with UBF1, but to a significantly lesser extent with RPA194.
claims.source: In contrast, the AMD-induced perinucleolar or nucleoplasmic solid condensates formed by the Δ83–1121 or CS Treacle mutants still co-localized with UBF1, but to a significantly lesser extent with RPA194 (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The condensates formed by Δ83–1121 or CS mutants after AMD treatment displace FBL and incorporate NCL.
claims.source: Interestingly, these condensates exhibited behavior opposite to that of full-length Treacle condensates with respect to FBL and NCL: they displaced FBL and incorporated NCL (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The disruption of Treacle's condensation properties results in a shift in its interaction repertoire, preserving interaction with UBF1, diminishing interactions with RNA Pol I and FBL, and establishing a new interaction with NCL.
claims.source: Thus, the disruption of Treacle's condensation properties, either through RD deletion or charge scrambling, results in a shift in its interaction repertoire. Specifically, while interaction with UBF1 is preserved, interactions with RNA Pol I and FBL are notably diminished, whereas a new interaction with NCL is established.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the altered co-localization patterns of condensation-defective mutants.

claims.claim: The correct condensation of Treacle contributes to the formation of the cooperative FC/DFC structure by mediating functional interactions with partner proteins.
claims.source: It is likely that the correct condensation of Treacle contributes to the formation of the cooperative FC/DFC structure by mediating functional interactions with partner proteins.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the altered interactions and loss of FC/DFC structure in condensation-defective mutants.

claims.claim: The expression of condensation-defective Treacle mutants significantly reduces the transcription of rRNA compared to full-length Treacle.
claims.source: We found that the expression of condensation-defective Treacle mutants significantly reduced the transcription of rRNA compared to full-length Treacle (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The reduced rRNA transcription in cells expressing condensation-defective Treacle mutants correlates with a reduced ability to maintain the association of partner proteins RPA194 and UBF1 at the rDNA promoter.
claims.source: This effect correlated with a reduced ability of condensation-defective Treacle mutants to maintain the association of partner proteins RPA194 and UBF1 at the rDNA promoter (Figure 6C), along with diminished intrinsic binding of these mutants to rDNA (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claims.claim: Condensation-defective Treacle mutants exhibit diminished intrinsic binding to rDNA.
claims.source: This effect correlated with a reduced ability of condensation-defective Treacle mutants to maintain the association of partner proteins RPA194 and UBF1 at the rDNA promoter (Figure 6C), along with diminished intrinsic binding of these mutants to rDNA (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The condensation properties of Treacle underlie its ability to concentrate components of the transcriptional machinery in the FC and separate them from the DFC.
claims.source: These observations suggest that the condensation properties of Treacle underlie its ability to concentrate components of the transcriptional machinery in the FC and separate them from the DFC.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the reduced transcription and altered localization in condensation-defective mutants.

claims.claim: The separation of FC and DFC is likely required to maintain highly efficient transcription of rDNA.
claims.source: Moreover, such separation is likely required to maintain highly efficient transcription of rDNA.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the reduced transcription efficiency when FC/DFC separation is lost.

claims.claim: Newly synthesized 47S pre-rRNA transcripts cluster at the periphery of FCs in full-length Treacle-expressing cells.
claims.source: Microscopy analyses with fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)-labeled rRNA revealed that newly synthesized 47S pre-rRNA transcripts clustered at the periphery of FCs in full-length Treacle-expressing cells, reflecting the radial flow of rRNA from the FC to the GC (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Newly synthesized rRNA is relocated to the periphery of large Treacle condensates formed at high expression levels.
claims.source: Newly synthesized rRNA was also relocated to the periphery of large Treacle condensates formed at high expression levels (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: No apparent clustering of newly synthesized rRNA is observed in cells expressing condensation-defective Treacle mutants.
claims.source: However, no apparent clustering of newly synthesized rRNA was observed in cells expressing condensation-defective Treacle mutants. Instead, the newly synthesized transcripts were diffusely mixed with Δ83–1121 and CS Treacle (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Nascent rRNA transcripts are mixed with delocalized UBF in cells depleted of endogenous Treacle.
claims.source: Nascent rRNA transcripts were similarly mixed with delocalized UBF in cells depleted of endogenous Treacle (Treacle kn; Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: Supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Cells overexpressing condensation-defective Treacle mutants have impaired 5′ external transcribed spacer processing compared to cells overexpressing full-length Treacle.
claims.source: Finally, reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) analysis confirmed that cells overexpressing condensation-defective Treacle mutants had impaired 5′ external transcribed spacer processing compared to cells overexpressing full-length Treacle (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Treacle's condensation properties separate the FC and DFC, leading to the spatial segregation of rRNA synthesis and subsequent processing.
claims.source: Our results indicate that Treacle's condensation properties separate the FC and DFC, leading to the spatial segregation of rRNA synthesis and subsequent processing.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the loss of spatial organization and processing defects in condensation-defective mutants.

claims.claim: The mixing of FC and DFC components due to the disruption of Treacle's condensation ability reduces the efficiency of both rRNA synthesis and processing.
claims.source: The mixing of FC and DFC components due to the disruption of Treacle's condensation ability reduces the efficiency of both processes, with equivalent effects to the complete depletion of endogenous Treacle.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the similar defects observed in condensation-defective mutants and Treacle-depleted cells.

claims.claim: Treating cells with 90 µM VP16 for 30 min results in the rapid recruitment of TOPBP1 to nucleoli and its co-localization with Treacle in HeLa cells.
claims.source: Treating cells with 90 µM VP16 for 30 min resulted in the rapid recruitment of TOPBP1 to nucleoli and its co-localization with Treacle in HeLa (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and MCF7 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 7A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: PLA analysis provides evidence of a physical association between TOPBP1 and Treacle after DNA damage induction.
claims.source: Furthermore, proximity ligation assay (PLA) analysis conducted after DNA damage induction provided evidence of a physical association between TOPBP1 and Treacle (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by PLA data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Reducing endogenous Treacle levels effectively blocks the relocalization of TOPBP1 to nucleoli.
claims.source: Reducing endogenous Treacle levels, either through RNA interference (Treacle kd) or CRISPR/Cas9-mediated depletion (Treacle kn), effectively blocked the relocalization of TOPBP1 to nucleoli (Figure 7D; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B) and its occupancy of rDNA (Figure 7C).

results.result: Treacle is essential for maintaining the tripartite nucleolar structure in human cells. In Treacle-positive cells, Treacle co-localizes with FC markers (UBF1, RPA194) in fibrillar centers, while FBL localizes to the DFC and B23/nucleolin surround the DFC. Depletion of Treacle causes disappearance of distinct FC and DFC structures, mixing of FC/DFC components, and partial redistribution of nucleolar proteins to the nucleoplasm, while minimally affecting GC organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 are well-supported by immunocytochemical staining data shown in Figure 1A-B and supplementary figures across multiple cell types (HeLa cells and human skin fibroblasts). The co-localization patterns are clearly demonstrated through microscopy images with quantitative line profile analysis. The structural changes upon Treacle depletion are consistently observed and documented with appropriate controls.

results.result: Treacle amplifies recruitment of transcription machinery to rDNA rather than initiating primary binding. ChIP analysis shows that Treacle depletion decreases occupancy of UBF and RPA194 within the rDNA coding region, while mock sgRNA transfection has no such effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 are supported by ChIP-qPCR data (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) showing reduced but not absent binding of transcription factors upon Treacle depletion. The mock sgRNA control appropriately demonstrates specificity. The interpretation that Treacle amplifies rather than initiates binding is reasonable given the partial reduction observed.

results.result: Treacle depletion substantially suppresses rDNA transcription and impairs 5′ external transcribed spacer processing, particularly at the A′ site cleavage step in 18S rRNA maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15 are supported by EU incorporation assays (Figure 1D-E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and RT-qPCR data (Figure 1F) with appropriate quantification. The distinction between substantial but incomplete suppression (unlike AMD-induced complete repression) is clearly demonstrated. Statistical significance is shown with appropriate replicates.

results.result: Treacle is a fully intrinsically disordered protein with three functional domains: N-terminal domain (ND) containing LisH motif and NLS, central repeating domain (RD) with 15 S/E-rich LCRs interspersed with linkers showing high homology, and C-terminal domain (CD) with additional NLSs, UBF binding site, and K-rich LCR functioning as NoLS.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21 are supported by computational predictions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and citations to established literature (Gál et al., 2022; Jaberi Lashkari et al., 2023). The structural characterization is consistent with known protein features and provides the foundation for subsequent functional studies. The domain organization is clearly illustrated in Figure 2A.

results.result: A recombinant Treacle fragment (amino acids 291–426) forms liquid-like condensates in vitro in the presence of 5% polyethylene glycol, exhibiting spherical morphology and frequent fusion events.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are directly supported by in vitro condensation assays shown in Figure 2B-C with microscopy images demonstrating spherical morphology and time-lapse imaging documenting fusion events. These are classic characteristics of liquid-liquid phase separation and provide strong evidence for Treacle's condensation capacity.

results.result: Opto-Treacle (Treacle-FusionRed-Cry2 fusion) forms foci in nucleoli in the absence of blue light and forms multiple small foci throughout the nucleoplasm under blue light illumination.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26 are supported by live-cell imaging data (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) with appropriate controls. The optogenetic approach provides additional evidence for Treacle's condensation properties and demonstrates light-inducible condensate formation, consistent with phase separation behavior.

results.result: Treacle fusion proteins form foci exclusively in nucleoli at low expression levels (16–24 hr post-transfection) but generate large spherical extranucleolar structures at high expression levels (48–72 hr post-transfection). These structures exhibit spherical morphology with aspect ratio close to one and internal homogeneity, independent of fluorescent protein oligomerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C31 are well-supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 2E, supplementary figures 1C-E), 3D shape analysis, and transmission electron microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F). The control experiment showing condensate formation without fluorescent protein tags (C29) is critical for ruling out artifacts. The spherical morphology and internal homogeneity are consistent with liquid-like condensates.

results.result: Nucleolar caps form during AMD-induced or DNA damage-induced rDNA transcriptional repression through fusion of intranucleolar Treacle foci. Extranucleolar condensates from highly overexpressed Treacle frequently fuse, indicating dynamic clustering.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 are supported by time-lapse imaging (Figure 2F-G, supplementary figures 1G-H, and associated videos). The fusion events are directly visualized and quantified, providing strong evidence for liquid-like behavior. The observation across different conditions (AMD treatment, DNA damage, overexpression) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: FRAP analysis reveals that Treacle condensates exhibit preferential internal mixing with slow external exchange. Half-FRAP shows fluorescence equilibration between bleached and non-bleached halves without significant boundary exchange. Full-FRAP shows slow recovery. Similar dynamics are observed for FCs, nucleolar caps, and smaller extranucleolar condensates, while the largest extranucleolar condensates show reduced dynamics suggesting gel-like properties and potential liquid-to-gel phase transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C40 are supported by comprehensive FRAP analysis (Figure 2H-M, supplementary figures 2A-D, and associated videos) across multiple condensate types. The half-FRAP and full-FRAP experiments are well-designed to distinguish internal mixing from boundary exchange. The observation of reduced dynamics in larger condensates (C39) and speculation about liquid-to-gel transition (C40) is reasonable but the latter is appropriately presented as speculation rather than established fact.

results.result: The Δ1–83 mutant (lacking N-terminal domain) demonstrates condensation properties indistinguishable from full-length Treacle, forming FCs, nucleolar caps, and extranucleolar condensates with high molecular exchange rates in all condensate types.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by microscopy data (Figure 3A and supplementary figures) and partial FRAP analysis (Figure 3B-C). The comprehensive characterization across multiple condensate models with quantitative FRAP measurements provides strong evidence that the N-terminal domain is dispensable for condensation.

results.result: The Δ83–1121 mutant (lacking repeating domain) exhibits significantly compromised condensation properties. At low expression, it fails to concentrate in FCs and diffusely localizes in nucleolus with high dynamics. During transcriptional repression, it forms nucleoplasmic condensates that transition to solid-like state. At high expression, it forms a unified pan-nuclear solid network rather than distinct condensates, suggesting altered interaction patterns with increased reliance on rRNA and nucleolar proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 are supported by microscopy (Figure 3D-F and supplementary figures) and FRAP data showing altered condensation behavior and liquid-to-solid transitions. The comprehensive characterization across expression levels and conditions demonstrates the critical role of the RD. The interpretation about altered interaction patterns (C48) is reasonable inference from the observed phenotypes.

results.result: The Δ1121–1488 mutant (lacking C-terminal domain) fails to condense. Even with artificial NLS from SV40, it successfully translocates to nucleus but remains diffusely distributed throughout nucleoplasm, indicating that the CD is required as a nucleation factor for autonomous condensation.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by microscopy data (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G). The use of artificial NLS is an appropriate control to separate localization from condensation defects. The conclusion that CD acts as nucleation factor (C51) is reasonable inference from the complete loss of condensation despite nuclear localization.

results.result: Intracellular Treacle condensation depends on cooperative interaction between RD and CD, with the ND playing negligible role. The K-rich LCR in CD facilitates nucleation while alternating charge blocks in RD stabilize condensates, ensuring Treacle behavior remains independent of subnuclear localization or transcriptional activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C71-C74 represent synthesis of findings from deletion mutant studies (C41-C51). The conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive characterization of Δ1–83, Δ83–1121, and Δ1121–1488 mutants. The cooperative model is consistent with all observed phenotypes and represents appropriate integration of the experimental data.

results.result: Treacle condensation is primarily governed by electrostatic interactions rather than hydrophobic forces. Treatment with ammonium acetate disrupts condensates while 1,6-HD has no effect, both in vitro and in vivo. In vitro condensation is also sensitive to pH changes, with optimal efficiency at pH 7.0.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 are supported by both cellular experiments (Figure 4A) and in vitro assays (Figure 4B) testing sensitivity to salt, 1,6-HD, and pH. The convergence of in vitro and in vivo results strengthens the conclusion about electrostatic interactions. The pH sensitivity data provides additional support for the role of charged residues.

results.result: Deletion of S/E-rich LCRs (ΔSE mutant) significantly compromises Treacle's condensation properties. Like Δ83–1121 mutant, ΔSE cannot form FCs or nucleolar caps, remains liquid in nucleolus, and undergoes liquid-solid phase transition during transcriptional repression or high overexpression, indicating that RD determines condensation properties through S/E-rich LCRs.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are supported by microscopy and FRAP data (Figure 4C-E and supplementary figures). The phenotypic similarity between ΔSE and Δ83–1121 mutants provides strong evidence that the S/E-rich LCRs are the critical functional elements within the RD. The conclusion (C61) is well-supported by the experimental observations.

results.result: The ΔNoLS mutant (lacking K-rich LCR) does not localize to nucleolus but forms individual perinucleolar condensates whose volume increases with expression level while number remains constant, suggesting limited nucleation sites. These condensates display high molecular dynamics with exchange across boundaries rather than internal mixing, indicating the K-rich LCR acts as both nucleation element and regulator of volumetric dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C67 are supported by microscopy (Figure 4F and supplementary figures) and FRAP data (Figure 4G-H and supplementary figures 1C-D). The observation of limited nucleation sites (C63) and altered exchange dynamics (C66) compared to full-length Treacle provides strong evidence for the dual role of K-rich LCR in nucleation and dynamics regulation (C67).

results.result: Each S/E-rich LCR with its adjacent linker constitutes a strong diblock ampholyte with positively charged linker followed by negatively charged LCR. Charge scrambling in RD (CS mutant) fully reproduces the condensation-defective phenotype of Δ83–1121 and ΔSE mutants, demonstrating that condensation properties depend not only on net negative charge but critically on specific charge distribution within RD.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by charge distribution analysis (Figure 4I) and microscopy data of CS mutant (Figure 4J and supplementary figures). The charge-scrambling experiment is a critical control that demonstrates the importance of charge patterning rather than just charge content. This is a sophisticated experimental design that strongly supports the diblock ampholyte model.

results.result: Full-length Treacle exhibits normal nucleolar localization and co-localizes with FC markers (RPA194, UBF) while FBL localizes to DFC periphery and NCL/B23 surround DFC. In contrast, Δ83–1121 or CS mutants cause dispersal and mixing of FC/DFC components, still co-localize with UBF1 but show reduced co-localization with RPA194, and show partial overlap with NCL but not B23, suggesting altered interaction preferences.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 are supported by immunocytochemical data with co-localization analysis (Figure 5A-B and supplementary figures). The quantitative line profile analysis provides objective assessment of co-localization patterns. The observation of differential effects on different protein interactions (preserved UBF1, reduced RPA194, new NCL interaction) is well-documented and supports the conclusion about altered interaction preferences.

results.result: After AMD treatment, full-length Treacle co-localizes with UBF1 and RPA194 at nucleolar caps, with FBL partially merging and NCL/B23 displaced. Condensation-defective mutants (Δ83–1121 or CS) show opposite behavior: still co-localize with UBF1 but reduced RPA194, displace FBL and incorporate NCL. This shift in interaction repertoire (preserved UBF1, diminished RNA Pol I and FBL, new NCL interaction) suggests correct condensation contributes to cooperative FC/DFC structure formation through mediating functional protein interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C86 are supported by immunocytochemical data after AMD treatment (Figure 5C-D and supplementary figures). The systematic comparison between full-length and condensation-defective mutants reveals consistent patterns of altered interactions. The conclusion that condensation properties mediate functional interactions (C86) is reasonable inference from the observed correlation between condensation defects and altered protein partnerships.

results.result: Expression of condensation-defective Treacle mutants significantly reduces rRNA transcription compared to full-length Treacle, correlating with reduced ability to maintain RPA194 and UBF1 association at rDNA promoter and diminished intrinsic binding to rDNA. This suggests condensation properties underlie Treacle's ability to concentrate transcriptional machinery in FC and separate from DFC, which is required for efficient rDNA transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 are supported by RT-qPCR (Figure 6A), ChIP-seq (Figure 6B), and ChIP-qPCR (Figure 6C) data with appropriate statistical analysis and replicates. The correlation between condensation defects, reduced protein recruitment, and decreased transcription is well-established. The mechanistic interpretation (C90-C91) is reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: Newly synthesized 47S pre-rRNA clusters at FC periphery in full-length Treacle-expressing cells and at periphery of large Treacle condensates, reflecting radial flow. In condensation-defective mutants or Treacle-depleted cells, rRNA is diffusely mixed without apparent clustering. Cells with condensation-defective mutants show impaired 5′ ETS processing. This indicates Treacle's condensation properties separate FC and DFC, enabling spatial segregation of rRNA synthesis and processing, with mixing reducing efficiency of both processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C98 are supported by smFISH data (Figure 6D-F) and RT-qPCR (Figure 6G) with clear visualization of rRNA localization patterns. The loss of spatial organization in condensation-defective mutants and correlation with processing defects provides strong evidence for the functional importance of FC/DFC separation. The mechanistic model (C97-C98) is well-supported by the comprehensive data.

results.result: VP16 treatment (90 µM, 30 min) results in rapid recruitment of TOPBP1 to nucleoli and co-localization with Treacle in HeLa and MCF7 cells, with physical association confirmed by PLA. Reducing endogenous Treacle levels through RNAi or CRISPR/Cas9 effectively blocks TOPBP1 relocalization to nucleoli and its occupancy of rDNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by immunocytochemical data (Figure 7A, 7D and supplementary figures), PLA analysis (Figure 7B and supplementary figures), and ChIP data (Figure 7C). The convergence of multiple techniques (immunofluorescence, PLA, ChIP) provides strong evidence for the interaction. The observation across two cell lines strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Expressing siRNA-resistant full-length Treacle in Treacle kd cells effectively restores VP16-induced Treacle-TOPBP1 interaction and TOPBP1 enrichment at rDNA promoters, while expressing condensation-defective forms (Δ83–1121 or CS) does not restore these interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 are supported by immunocytochemical analysis and ChIP data (Figure 7E-F and supplementary figures). The rescue experiment with full-length Treacle and failure to rescue with condensation-defective mutants provides strong evidence that condensation properties are required for TOPBP1 interaction. This is a well-designed experiment with appropriate controls.

results.result: VP16 induces DDR at rDNA promoters including ATM/ATR activation, H2AX phosphorylation, and 53BP1/BRCA1 recruitment. Nucleolar DDR is fully controlled by Treacle-TOPBP1 interaction, as knockdown of either protein dramatically reduces VP16-induced repair signaling. DDR can be restored by overexpressing full-length Treacle but not condensation-defective mutants, indicating Treacle's phase separation is crucial for TOPBP1 binding and DDR activation in response to genotoxic damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 are supported by comprehensive ChIP-qPCR analysis of multiple DDR markers (Figure 7G-H and supplementary figures) with appropriate controls including knockdowns and rescue experiments. The systematic demonstration that condensation-defective mutants cannot restore DDR despite having intact phosphoserines 1227/1228 (mentioned in discussion) provides strong evidence that phase separation is required for functional TOPBP1 interaction.

results.result: Treacle serves as scaffold protein for nucleolar FCs in human cells, consistent with evolutionary correlation between Treacle emergence and three-partite nucleolus appearance in amniotes. Introducing human Treacle into zebrafish induces reorganization from bipartite to tripartite nucleolar structure with FC-like structure formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 integrate findings from the current study (loss of FC structure upon Treacle depletion) with cited literature (Jaberi Lashkari et al., 2023) on evolutionary and cross-species observations. While C110 is stated as established knowledge rather than data from this study, the overall conclusion about Treacle as FC scaffold (C108) is well-supported by the comprehensive structural and functional data presented.

results.result: Treacle's condensation properties are governed by synergistic interplay between RD and CD. While RD can form liquid-like condensates alone in vitro, its cellular condensation requires positively charged CD as nucleation platform. Zebrafish Treacle ortholog shows sequence homology only in RD, lacking homologous CD sequence, likely accounting for its inability to undergo condensation and form FC-like structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 are well-supported by the comprehensive deletion mutant analysis and in vitro studies. C114-C115 integrate current findings with cited literature (Hill-Terán et al., 2024) to provide evolutionary context. The model of RD-CD cooperation is strongly supported by the experimental data, though the zebrafish comparison (C114-C115) relies on cited work rather than direct experimental evidence in this study.

results.result: Treacle functions as block polyampholyte with condensation governed by alternating charges in RD and positive charge in CD, likely driven by coacervation mechanisms. Both homotypic (through K-rich LCR/E-rich LCR interactions and E-rich LCR/K-rich linker dynamics) and heterotypic (with UBF and RNA Pol I) coacervation may drive Treacle condensation. Charge scrambling or RD deletion partially disrupts RNA Pol I interaction, reduces rDNA recruitment, and impairs condensation.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C120 represent reasonable mechanistic interpretation supported by charge distribution analysis (Figure 4I) and sensitivity to electrostatic disruption. C121-C122 are appropriately presented as speculative mechanisms. C123-C124 integrate current findings with cited literature on partner protein properties. C125 provides experimental support for the heterotypic interaction model through co-localization and ChIP data. The overall model is well-reasoned though some aspects remain speculative.

results.result: Endogenous Treacle undergoes post-translational modifications (phosphorylation and ubiquitination in RD). Phosphorylation can modulate phase separation by altering polyampholytic properties. Post-translational modifications may fine-tune Treacle's condensation properties by modulating partner interactions and altering RD ampholytic properties through charge ratio changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C127 are supported by cited literature (Mooser et al., 2020; Werner et al., 2015, 2018; Yamazaki et al., 2022) establishing that Treacle is modified and that PTMs can affect phase separation. However, C128 is explicitly speculative and no direct experimental evidence is provided in this study testing the effects of PTMs on Treacle condensation. This represents a reasonable hypothesis for future work but is not experimentally validated here.

results.result: 47S pre-rRNA is synthesized at FC/DFC boundary with primary processing beginning in DFC. DFC formation is mediated by FBL phase separation on rRNA scaffold maintained by radial rRNA flow. While Treacle's role in rRNA processing has been described, the mechanism was unclear. Impaired processing in condensation-defective mutants correlates with loss of FBL association, increased rRNA/nucleolin association, and FC/DFC disorganization, which may compromise radial rRNA flow and hinder normal processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131 represent established knowledge supported by cited literature (Wu et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2019; Calo et al., 2018; Gonzales et al., 2005). C132-C134 integrate this knowledge with current findings on condensation-defective mutants. The mechanistic model linking FC/DFC disorganization to impaired processing (C134) is reasonable inference from the spatial organization and processing defect data, though the causal relationship could be more directly tested.

results.result: TOPBP1 plays crucial role in activating ATR during DNA replication stress, and its interaction with Treacle (via phosphoserines 1227/1228 in CD) is essential for nucleolar DDR. However, Treacle with intact phosphoserines but unable to condense loses ability to interact with TOPBP1 during genotoxic stress, indicating that Treacle's interaction with TOPBP1 and nucleolar DDR activation requires phase separation ability.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C137 are supported by cited literature (Day et al., 2021; Mooser et al., 2020; Velichko et al., 2019). C138-C139 represent key findings from this study showing that condensation-defective mutants (which retain phosphoserines 1227/1228) fail to interact with TOPBP1 and activate DDR. This is strong evidence that phase separation is required beyond the known phosphorylation sites, representing an important mechanistic advance.

results.result: Treacle serves as nucleolar hub protein integrating functions in rDNA transcription, rRNA processing, and rDNA repair, functioning not only as structural scaffold for FC/DFC.
results.evaluation: Claim C140 represents the overarching conclusion synthesizing all major findings of the study. It is well-supported by the comprehensive demonstration of Treacle's roles in: (1) FC/DFC structure formation, (2) transcription machinery recruitment and rDNA transcription, (3) rRNA processing through spatial organization, and (4) DDR activation through TOPBP1 interaction. The integration of these functions through phase separation properties is the central contribution of this work.

results.result: Treacle depletion disrupts the tripartite nucleolar structure, causing loss of distinct FC and DFC compartments, mixing of FC and DFC components, and redistribution of nucleolar proteins to the nucleoplasm, while minimally affecting the GC component. This demonstrates Treacle's critical role in forming the integrated FC/DFC structure.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge the strength of the characterization of nucleolar morphology changes upon Treacle knockout. Reviewer 2 specifically notes 'The characterizations of changes to nuclear morphology upon Treacle knockout is the strength of this study' and that the data 'support the idea that Treacle has a scaffolding function.' The editor states the study 'provides convincing evidence' for Treacle's role in proper FC formation.

results.result: Treacle depletion decreases the occupancy of UBF and RPA194 at rDNA, substantially suppresses rDNA transcription, and impairs 5' external transcribed spacer processing, suggesting Treacle amplifies recruitment of transcription machinery rather than initiating primary binding.
results.evaluation: The editor states the study provides 'convincing evidence' for Treacle's necessity in 'rRNA transcription.' Reviewer 1 notes the study is 'important for our understanding of the role of Treacle in nucleolar organization and function.' No reviewer challenges these functional claims about transcription and processing.

results.result: Treacle is a fully intrinsically disordered protein with three functional domains: N-terminal domain (with LisH motif and NLS), central repeat domain (with 15 S/E-rich LCRs interspersed with linkers), and C-terminal domain (with NLSs, UBF binding site, and K-rich LCR/NoLS).
results.evaluation: These structural characterizations are not challenged by any reviewer. The domain organization is accepted as background for understanding condensation properties. Reviewer 2 specifically discusses 'the charge-segregated central region of Treacle' in their evaluation, implicitly accepting this structural description.

results.result: A recombinant fragment of Treacle (amino acids 291–426) forms liquid-like condensates in vitro with spherical morphology that undergo fusion events in the presence of 5% polyethylene glycol.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a significant concern: 'The conclusion that Treacle is a core scaffold of the FC is weakly supported. Recombinant Treacle has intrinsic potential to condense...It should be kept in mind that all proteins will condense at sufficiently high concentrations and under crowding. The authors observed condensation at 100uM protein and 5% PEG8000.' This suggests the in vitro condensation data alone are insufficient to establish physiological relevance.

results.result: Opto-Treacle and Treacle fusion proteins form concentration-dependent condensates in cells: nucleolar foci at low expression, large extranucleolar spherical structures at high expression, and nucleolar caps during transcriptional repression. These structures exhibit spherical morphology, internal homogeneity, and undergo fusion events.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 specifically praises 'the overexpression studies, done in the absence of endogenous protein and accounted for the protein expression levels.' The editor notes the study 'reveals that the nucleolar protein Treacle undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation in vitro and in vivo,' accepting the cellular condensation data. No reviewer challenges these observations.

results.result: FRAP analysis reveals that Treacle condensates exhibit internal mixing without significant exchange across boundaries, with slow recovery rates in full-FRAP. The largest extranucleolar condensates show reduced dynamics suggesting gel-like properties and potential liquid-to-gel phase transition.
results.evaluation: The FRAP characterization is not challenged by reviewers. Reviewer 3 notes 'In vitro and in vivo experiments highlight that Treacle is itself capable of undergoing condensation' and praises the 'high quality' data and 'well-designed' experiments. The dynamic properties are accepted as part of the condensation characterization.

results.result: Domain deletion analysis shows that the Δ1-83 mutant behaves like full-length Treacle, while Δ83-1121 (lacking RD) and Δ1121-1488 (lacking CD) exhibit compromised condensation. The RD deletion causes diffuse nucleolar localization and liquid-solid transitions, while CD deletion prevents autonomous condensation, indicating cooperative interaction between RD and CD governs Treacle condensation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically highlights 'The attempts to generate separation-of-function mutants to dissect the contribution of condensation to Treacle function are ambitious and critical to demonstrating the relevance of this property to the biology of the FC.' Reviewer 2 notes the study provides 'new insight into the role played by the charge-segregated central region of Treacle in terms of having the potential to undergo condensation.' The domain analysis is viewed as a strength.

results.result: Treacle condensation is disrupted by salt (ammonium acetate) but not by 1,6-hexanediol, and is sensitive to pH changes, indicating condensation is governed by electrostatic interactions rather than hydrophobic forces.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'Treacle is itself capable of undergoing condensation in a manner that depends on concentration and charge-charge interactions, but is not affected by 1,6 hexanediol.' This explicitly accepts the mechanistic characterization. The sensitivity to expected solution conditions is acknowledged by Reviewer 2 without challenging the interpretation.

results.result: Deletion of S/E-rich LCRs (ΔSE mutant) compromises condensation similar to Δ83-1121, while deletion of the K-rich LCR (ΔNoLS mutant) prevents nucleolar localization but allows formation of limited perinucleolar condensates with altered dynamics. This indicates the RD determines condensation through S/E-rich LCRs, while the K-rich LCR acts as nucleation element and regulator of dynamics.
results.evaluation: These fine-mapping experiments are part of the separation-of-function mutant analysis praised by Reviewer 3 as 'ambitious and critical.' Reviewer 2 specifically mentions 'the charge scramble mutant' as a strength, indicating acceptance of the charge-based mechanistic dissection. No concerns are raised about these specific mutant characterizations.

results.result: Charge distribution analysis shows each S/E-rich LCR with adjacent linker forms a diblock ampholyte. Charge scrambling (CS mutant) reproduces the condensation-defective phenotype, demonstrating that condensation depends on specific charge distribution, not just net charge. The RD and CD cooperatively govern phase separation, with the K-rich LCR facilitating nucleation and alternating charge blocks stabilizing condensates.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically highlights 'the characterization of the effects of the charge scramble mutant' as a strength, noting it 'reduces the bulk dynamics of Treacle as assessed by FRAP, de-mixes FBL from the DFC, lowers pre-rRNA synthesis, and abolishes the recruitment of the DNA-damage response factor TOPBP1.' This indicates acceptance of the charge scrambling approach and its mechanistic implications.

results.result: Full-length Treacle maintains proper FC/DFC organization and co-localizes with RPA194, UBF, and FBL, while condensation-defective mutants (Δ83-1121, CS) cause dispersal and mixing of FC/DFC components, alter interaction patterns (preserving UBF1 interaction but diminishing RPA194 and FBL interactions while establishing new NCL interaction), suggesting condensation mediates functional protein interactions.
results.evaluation: The altered interaction patterns of condensation-defective mutants are accepted as part of the functional characterization. Reviewer 2 notes these mutants 'de-mix FBL from the DFC,' accepting the co-localization analysis. Reviewer 3 states the findings 'tie to a role in maintaining separation of FC components from the DFC,' supporting the interpretation that condensation mediates proper organization.

results.result: Condensation-defective Treacle mutants significantly reduce rRNA transcription, decrease recruitment of RPA194 and UBF1 to rDNA, exhibit diminished rDNA binding, impair rRNA processing, and cause loss of spatial segregation of rRNA synthesis and processing. This demonstrates that Treacle's condensation properties are required for efficient rDNA transcription and proper rRNA processing through spatial organization.
results.evaluation: The editor states the study provides 'convincing evidence that the ability of Treacle to form phase-separated condensates is necessary for...rRNA transcription.' Reviewer 2 notes condensation-defective mutants 'lower pre-rRNA synthesis,' accepting the functional link. Reviewer 3 states the authors 'provide evidence that these same protein forms are also disrupted in supporting Treacle's functions in rDNA transcription and rRNA processing,' explicitly supporting these claims.

results.result: VP16-induced DNA damage recruits TOPBP1 to nucleoli where it co-localizes and physically associates with Treacle. Treacle depletion blocks TOPBP1 relocalization, and condensation-defective Treacle mutants fail to restore TOPBP1 interaction and nucleolar DDR activation, demonstrating that Treacle's phase separation is crucial for TOPBP1 binding and DDR activation at rDNA.
results.evaluation: The editor states the study provides 'convincing evidence' for Treacle's necessity in 'rDNA repair.' Reviewer 2 notes condensation-defective mutants 'abolish the recruitment of the DNA-damage response factor TOPBP1,' accepting this functional link. Reviewer 3 acknowledges the authors 'suggest that cells lacking Treacle are defective in the DNA damage response at the rDNA' but notes 'further studies will be required to fully explore the relevance of Treacle condensation to the stability of the rDNA repeats,' indicating the basic finding is accepted but mechanistic details require further work.

results.result: Treacle serves as the scaffold protein for nucleolar FCs through phase separation governed by synergistic RD-CD interaction. The RD can condense in vitro but requires the CD for cellular condensation. Treacle functions as a block polyampholyte driven by coacervation mechanisms (both homotypic and heterotypic), with potential modulation by post-translational modifications. Evolutionary emergence of Treacle correlates with tripartite nucleolus appearance.
results.evaluation: These mechanistic and evolutionary interpretations are accepted by reviewers as part of the overall narrative. Reviewer 1 states the study is 'important for our understanding of the role of Treacle in nucleolar organization and function, as well as general principles of cellular compartmentalization that involve biomolecular condensates.' The editor notes findings 'will be of interest to the communities studying biomolecular condensates, nucleolar organization, and ribosome biogenesis,' accepting the broader implications.

results.result: Treacle integrates multiple nucleolar functions (rDNA transcription, rRNA processing, rDNA repair) as a hub protein. The impairment of rRNA processing in condensation-defective mutants correlates with loss of FBL association and altered rRNA/nucleolin interactions, suggesting Treacle's condensation maintains the radial flow of rRNA from FC to DFC required for efficient processing.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'The complementarity of the methods applied to investigate Treacle function are appropriate and the findings integrate well towards a compelling narrative,' accepting the integrated functional model. The editor's statement that the study demonstrates Treacle's necessity for 'rRNA transcription, and rDNA repair' supports the hub protein concept. No reviewer challenges the integration of these functions.
